Society & Human Rights
• Kenya’s Paul Mackenzie received an effective life/200-year sentence for ordering followers to starve 191 people, mostly children, in a “doomsday” cult.  
• Tanzania’s detained opposition figure was convicted of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason; he says the case is political.  
• Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault in London; industry fallout includes a producer stepping back and public reactions from Bear Grylls.  
• UK debates over historical slavery intensified after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch’s remarks opposing an apology; separate scrutiny grows over extending Palantir’s NHS contract while pursuing a domestic alternative.  
• Protests hit Microsoft’s Amsterdam data-center site; Afghan refugee women cricketers criticized foreign players for joining Afghanistan’s league; reports allege K-pop group NewJeans’ contracts removed key child protections.  
Why it matters: Rights, justice and accountability debates are surfacing across politics, culture and tech infrastructure, with implications for public trust and corporate conduct.

Armed Conflict & Security
• A fresh wave of bomb threats disrupted at least 18 European flights and media outlets; no explosives were found, and officials call it likely a coordinated disruption campaign.  
• Ukraine raised the death toll to at least 50 from a strike on a Zaporizhia aid site; dozens remain trapped as DNA tests identify victims.  
• Analysis warns Houthi child recruitment is shaping a generation in Yemen; separately, a Linux “aSSHole” flaw may allow passwordless SSH logins on some devices.  
Why it matters: Security threats—from hoaxes to warfare and cyber vulnerabilities—strain institutions and civilians while demanding coordinated responses.

Art & Culture
• Diwali celebrations lit up India as families marked the festival with lamps, fireworks and sweets amid air-quality concerns in Delhi.  
• Hundreds of 26,000-year-old cave engravings were identified in a popular site, including indications of “animated” sequences.  
• Torino Film Festival highlights female directors and unveils a Marilyn Monroe centenary retrospective framing her as a “female Marlon Brando.”  
Why it matters: Cultural heritage and festivals shape identity, while festivals influence industry trends and narratives around iconic figures.

Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Indonesia is roiled by a presidential wiretapping scandal implicating senior officials, exposing rifts among elites.  
• Somalia’s top court rejected the president’s term extension, casting doubt on the country’s first nationwide elections since 1969.  
• Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials urging a lasting Ukraine truce, while Iran intensified diplomacy amid US threats to resume war.  
• Pope Leo XIV began a three-nation Latin America trip three weeks after lung cancer surgery, with personal stops in Uruguay and Peru.  
• Paraguay’s president was impeached minutes after resigning amid a digital-bank collapse; US midterm outcomes reverberate globally, rattling tech-aligned political strategies.  
Why it matters: Political shocks and diplomatic maneuvers are reshaping alignments, ceasefire prospects and economic stability across regions.

Artificial Intelligence
• Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production in 2026 to free capacity for its driverless Cybercab, underscoring an AI-first shift.  
• AI “agents” accelerated: Airbnb plans an AI travel agent by 2027; Perplexity launched workplace agents; Meta’s Muse adds real-time voice and avatar calls.  
• OpenAI released a new cybersecurity model (GPT-6 Cyber), signaled openness to communities by stepping back from NDAs on data centers, and said it could be IPO-ready in 2027.  
• Google drew criticism for bundling AI into school search; Anthropic’s Claude can analyze personal finances via Plaid; reports detail chatbots’ growing ad experiments.  
• Chip access and geopolitics collide as China’s Moonshot AI seeks European routes to Nvidia hardware amid US export curbs.  
Why it matters: AI is moving from pilots to consumer and enterprise infrastructure, triggering policy, security and supply-chain debates.

Climate & Environment
• Delhi’s air turned “hazardous” days before Diwali, spotlighting chronic winter smog and health risks.  
• 2026 is likely to be the second-hottest year on record as a rapidly developing “super El Niño” boosts human-driven warming.  
• China’s Q3 CO2 emissions fell 3.1%, the biggest drop since Covid, amid energy and geopolitical shocks.  
• COP31 approaches with debates on fossil-fuel roadmaps and just transition; Europe signals support for a structured phase-down approach.  
• Studies highlight outsize methane from low-producing US wells and possible microplastics altering Pacific Ocean color.  
Why it matters: Escalating climate signals and policy choices will shape near-term health, energy prices and long-term transition pathways.

Economy & Markets
• The US added 165,000 jobs in October, beating forecasts and signaling a resilient labor market despite turbulence.  
• Tech-led market routs erased trillions in value, with AI stocks hit by political backlash over data centers, higher rates and return concerns.

• Musk-linked firms lost over $420bn in combined market cap post-midterms; oil slipped below $100 as traders recalibrated geopolitical risk.

Science & Technology
• Blue Origin unveiled a higher-performing, lower-cost engine and a third stage for New Glenn but pushed its next launch to January 2027 after a pad explosion.  
• NASA introduced the X-70 “Fractal” experimental aircraft and is soliciting ideas to extend Hubble’s life as its orbit decays.  
• Humanoid robots moved from demo to service as a startup cleaned homes in San Francisco; consumer tech buzz included a standout $649 3D printer and a minimalist “Enough Phone.”  
• The ISS completed next-gen roll-out solar arrays, while a large coronal hole could push northern lights as far south as New York and Idaho this weekend.  
• Research highlights: earliest direct evidence of cannabis use (2,800 years ago) and fresh signs of active volcanism on Mars.  
Why it matters: Spaceflight and aerospace advances continue amid delays, while robotics and new findings reshape consumer tech and planetary science.

Health & Pandemic
• “Make America Healthy Again” suffered major midterm losses, raising questions about the movement’s future.  
• Rising grocery prices are linked to higher food insufficiency and worse mental health; studies suggest social media could improve disaster-aid coordination and that better-designed flood warnings speed decisions.  
• Digital supports showed promise: online literacy instruction benefited autistic children, and a seven-week program improved dementia caregivers’ outlook and competence.  
Why it matters: Economic stressors and smarter communication tools are directly affecting public health and disaster resilience, while digital care models expand access.

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• A Nature Aging study identified vanadyl sulfate as a senolytic targeting altered cysteine reactivity, improving age-related conditions and extending lifespan in mice.  
• An NAD+ precursor failed in a Parkinson’s trial, underscoring the gap between mechanistic promise and clinical outcomes.  
• In mice, inhibiting the H3K9me3 epigenetic mark reduced Alzheimer’s pathology; a small trial of NOVOS Core was associated with improved arterial function and systolic blood pressure.  
• Analysts argue for better evaluation of lactoferrin’s geroprotective potential; Sweden’s Göteborg Film Festival will probe society’s fixation on youth in its “Forever Young” focus.  
Why it matters: Translating aging biology into safe, effective human therapies is progressing unevenly, spotlighting the need for rigorous trials and realistic expectations.

Society & Human Rights.title: Secret Deals Expose HYBE and ADOR's Firm Grip on K-Pop Sensation NewJeans
Society & Human Rights.text: SummaryAn investigation by The New York Times reveals restrictive confidential contracts signed by NewJeans under ADOR and HYBEThe agreements omitted standard government child protections while imposing severe behavioral conduct clauses and heavy exit penaltiesProvisions grant the label perpetual rights to the members' likenesses and AI-generated voice clones beyond the contract termAn investigative report into confidential agreements signed by record-breaking K-pop group NewJeans has revealed the extraordinary level of institutional control exerted by label ADOR and parent conglomerate HYBE. The New York Times obtained contracts—signed when members were between ages 14 and 17—which exposed how standard protections were stripped away beneath the surface of the group’s global commercial rise.According to the documents, the contracts removed key safeguards established in the South Korean government’s standard entertainment template, including guarantees for basic human rights, mental and physical health, education, and limits on excessive working hours. Instead, the agreements introduced strict behavioral mandates barring an “insincere attitude,” “neglect of self-management,” “inappropriate romantic relationships,” and making statements that could harm the company’s reputation. “This contract is unusually aggressive,” stated Seoul-based entertainment lawyer Jong-eon Roh. “It restricts the artists’ freedom to a degree rarely seen, even in recent major-label contracts.” U.S. entertainment attorney Dina LaPolt emphasized the stark industry contrast, noting, “In K-pop, you either do what they say, dress as they say, do your hair as they say, or you’re going to get replaced.”The contracts also enforced aggressive financial mechanisms, requiring members to repay trainee-era cosmetic procedures and establishing calculated exit penalties that only factor in profitable months. Following the group's attempted exit—which member Hanni Pham framed by stating, “Staying at the company will only prolong our psychological pain”—ADOR terminated member Danielle Marsh in December 2025 and filed a roughly $22 million USD lawsuit over unauthorized solo appearances. Marsh’s attorney, Jung Jong-chae, condemned the action to the Fair Trade Commission as an industry-wide warning: “If you try to escape Hybe’s control, this is the price you will pay.” Additionally, the terms grant the agency the right to indefinitely license the members' likenesses, repackage recordings at reduced royalty rates, and deploy AI-generated voice clones even after the contracts expire in 2029.In response, HYBE representatives stated that its contracts are legal, negotiated in good faith with parental consent, fully compliant with child-protection statutes, and structured to protect both talent and substantial corporate investments.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Art Collaboration Kyoto Spotlights Global Gallery Partnerships
Art & Culture.text: SummaryThe 2026 edition brings together 63 galleries from 18 countries and regions, spotlighting collaborations between Japanese and international galleries.Beyond the fair, visitors can explore experimental installations, artist talks, and exhibitions across Kyoto’s historic temples and cultural landmarks.Art Collaboration Kyoto (ACK) returns for its sixth edition from November 7 to 9, bringing together 63 galleries from 18 countries and regions at the Kyoto International Conference Center. With an expanded international presence and a newly established leadership structure, the 2026 fair continues its mission of fostering cross-cultural exchange between Japan's contemporary art scene and the wider global art community.At the heart of ACK are two signature sections: Gallery Collaborations and Kyoto Meetings. The former pairs Japanese galleries with international counterparts in shared exhibition spaces, encouraging dialogue across artistic practices and cultural perspectives. This year's participants include Tokyo's NANZUKA, which joins forces with New York's Jeffrey Deitch, TARO NASU with Hauser & Wirth, and Tokyo Gallery + BTAP with Seoul's Gallery Hyundai. Meanwhile, Kyoto Meetings spotlights artists and works connected to the historic city, with presentations from galleries including Perrotin, Art Court Gallery, and Kiang Malingue.Beyond the gallery presentations, ACK introduces ACK Intersections, a curated exhibition led by Leonhard Bartolomeus of the Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media (YCAM). Titled Out of Bounds, the program explores the invisible boundaries that shape our relationships with art, architecture, and one another. Featuring works by Ernesto Neto, Efrain Almeida, Piotr Kowalski, and others, the exhibition activates the Kyoto International Conference Center's distinctive architectural spaces. Additional programming includes installations by Aiko Miyanaga, Eriko Mukai, and Ryunosuke Okazaki, alongside a series of conversations featuring influential figures such as Arthur Jafa, Kazuyo Sejima, and Tomio Koyama.The fair's cultural footprint also extends throughout Kyoto through its What's On initiative, which highlights exhibitions staged across the city's galleries, temples, and historic landmarks. Among the presentations are exhibitions featuring Andrew Cranston at Ryosokuin Temple, Issy Wood and Evelyn Taocheng Wang at Daitokuji Temple's Korin-in and Yuka Kashiwabara at Komyoin Temple.Blending contemporary artistic perspectives with Kyoto's rich cultural heritage, ACK offers an alternative approach to the traditional art fair model, one that prioritizes collaboration, experimentation, and meaningful connections across borders.Art Collaboration Kyoto runs from November 7 to 9, 2026, at the Kyoto International Conference Center, view the full exhibitor list here.Kyoto International Conference Center422 Iwakura Osagicho, Sakyo-ku,Kyoto 606-0001, JapanClick here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Climate & Environment.text: Further south this week, severe thunderstorms affected midterms voting in Florida, Oklahoma and ColoradoDespite the rapid descent into autumn in the northern hemisphere, parts of eastern North America have experienced an exceptionally late taste of summer in recent days. Temperatures approached 23C (73F) in New York and Boston, about 7-10C above what is expected in early November. The unseasonable warmth spilled into parts of eastern Canada, with temperatures exceeding 20C, about 10-15C above normal for the time of year. The balmy conditions were caused by an area of low pressure in the US midwest, dragging up exceptionally warm air from the Gulf of Mexico along its eastern flank. This area of low pressure will gradually drift eastwards, allowing temperatures to fall closer to the average.Further south, severe thunderstorms have resulted in numerous flood warnings and evacuation warnings being issued this week across many states, with disruptive weather affecting polling stations in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado. The powerful thunderstorms even resulted in a tornado touching down in Keyes, Oklahoma, forcing the relocation of a polling station. Economy & Markets.title: Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion
Economy & Markets.text: This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!Hard work rarely speaks for itself.When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).That plan stalled my career for about five years.I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”Honestly, it never occurred to me.I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).Today, I would take a different approach. Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late. Now is a great time to start the conversation.Hard work is invisible by defaultEngineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.Just askBragging builds the case. Asking forces action.If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)When the answer is “no”Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you. Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.—BrianI Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Economy & Markets.title: Nintendo Switch 2 Sales Drop Nearly 40% After a Price Hike
Economy & Markets.text: SummaryNintendo experienced a 37.4 percent year-over-year decline in Switch 2 hardware sales during the first two quarters of its fiscal year following a price hikeDespite the drop in console adoption, operating profits surged 49.1 percent to $1.3 billion due to heavy software and multimedia momentumThe brand maintained its projection of 16.5 million hardware units for the current fiscal year, comfortably offsetting the launch-window cool-offThe post-launch honeymoon phase is officially cooling down for Nintendo. Over the first two quarters of its fiscal year, ending on September 30, sales of the Switch 2 fell by 37.4 percent compared with the exact same period last year. During this six-month stretch, the Japanese gaming giant moved 6.49 million units of the next-generation console. Breaking down that shifting momentum, Nintendo shipped 3.82 million units in the first quarter before slowing to 2.67 million units in the second quarter. The sharp hardware decline stands in contrast to the 10.36 million consoles sold during the same six-month window in the previous fiscal year, a surge driven by initial demand after the hardware originally launched on June 5, 2025.A major catalyst for this hardware dip arrived in early May, when Nintendo raised the price of the Switch 2 by $50 USD, bringing the retail cost up to $500 USD in the US. The brand attributed the premium to escalating memory costs alongside complex US tariffs. Nintendo noted that tariffs related to refunds were primarily borne directly by the company, rather than being passed on to consumers through product prices. The resulting drop in hardware unit sales took a toll on revenue streams, with Nintendo reporting a 12.1 percent decrease in overall net sales for the six months ended September 30, 2026. This financial downturn was primarily driven by reduced hardware output, which brought down the company's dedicated video game platform segment by 15.3 percent to $5.7 billion USD.Despite the drop in console adoption, the financial architecture behind the brand proved resilient. In contrast to the hardware decline, Nintendo saw its operating profit surge by 49.1 percent, climbing to ¥216.5 billion JPY, or approximately $1.3 billion USD. Overall net profit also rose 11 percent from a year earlier. This bottom-line expansion was supported by a strategic first-quarter US tariff refund and heavy cultural crossover success. Blockbuster software sales from titles like Splatoon Raiders paired with the mainstream popularity of the latest Super Mario movie, providing a diversified revenue safety net. Through these combined media avenues, total lifetime software sales for the Switch 2 reached 73.21 million units by September 30.Looking ahead, Nintendo maintained its baseline forecast, projecting it will move 16.5 million Switch 2 units for the current fiscal year. While that 16.5 million unit target is almost 17 percent lower than the 19.86 million consoles the company sold last year, holding steady on this projection reflects its overall hardware strategy. Nintendo's decision to maintain its initial hardware forecast despite the sales drop suggests the executive team had already factored fading launch-window hype and the planned price hike into its fiscal year projections. Because strong performance in its software and multimedia divisions allowed the company to offset the decline in console adoption, the Switch 2 reached a total of 26.35 million lifetime hardware units sold as of the close of the second quarter.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Science & Technology.title: Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras
Science & Technology.text: The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are. Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav ŠirokýDuring totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.A Mathematician’s Path to Solar Eclipse PhotographyDruckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.Miloslav DruckmüllerHe photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.Václav Široký and Miloslav DruckmüllerDespite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.What Solar Eclipses Reveal About the CoronaThe corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.How Eclipse Images Sparked a Scientific PartnershipWhen Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.How Image Processing Reveals the Solar CoronaCapturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.Václav ŠirokýTo create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.Choosing a Location for Solar Eclipse PhotographySince 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.Martin Šebek“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup. If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav ŠirokýOn the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.Mapping the Solar Corona’s Temperature With Iron The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona. Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav ŠirokýThose instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding. The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.Three, Two, One…TotalityWith just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”  The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav ŠirokýBut for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Entertainment.title: Sony Reports a 44% Jump in Quarterly Net Profit Driven by 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' and PlayStation
Entertainment.text: SummarySony reported a 44 percent net profit increase in Q2 2026, reaching $2.84 billionSpider-Man: Brand New Day drove a massive 527 percent jump in Sony Pictures earningsPlayStation software sales climbed despite hardware dips and an organized player blackoutOn November 5, Sony published its Q2 earnings materials for the 2026 fiscal year, revealing a massive financial surge driven by its entertainment and gaming divisions. The conglomerate reported net profits of ¥449.60 billion JPY, or approximately $2.84 billion USD, for the three months ending in September. Those numbers represented a steep 44 percent increase compared to the 311.4 billion yen, or roughly $1.96 billion, reported during the same period in 2025. This profit spike was largely fueled by its PlayStation business and the massive theatrical dominance of Spider-Man: Brand New Day.The cinematic return of the web-slinger completely reshaped the balance sheet for the film wing of the company. Released in July, Spider-Man: Brand New Day obliterated the global box office, taking in $2.52 billion during its theatrical run. That massive haul officially cemented the project as the third-highest grossing movie in history. Consequently, Sony Pictures Entertainment posted earnings of $581 million for the three months ended September. The Pictures division’s earnings marked a 527 percent jump from the $93 million reported for the same period in 2025.Over in the interactive division, the financial reality presented a stark split between hardware adoption and software consumption. Sales of PlayStation 5 consoles fell to 2.6 million units during the second quarter. By comparison, Sony sold 4 million PlayStation 5 units during Q2 2025. However, overall PlayStation game sales increased across both digital downloads and physical discs. The high-profile, Sony-exclusive game Marvel’s Wolverine generated significant commercial traction, selling 2.4 million units worldwide against a reported development budget of $300 million.That upward trajectory in software sales carries profound implications for the brand, as the overall growth occurred despite a week-long player blackout organized in August. The widespread protest was explicitly formed to push back against Sony's overarching plans to phase out physical game discs entirely. Continued software growth through active consumer friction suggests that the broader PlayStation ecosystem remains highly resilient as it prepares for its next era. Looking ahead to that hardware pipeline, Sony CFO Lin Tao stated that developers are currently making "solid progress" on the company's next-generation PlayStation console, confirming that the platform is "progressing as scheduled."Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Electronic Arts Launches 25 Classic PC Games on Steam for the First Time
Entertainment.text: SummaryElectronic Arts dropped 25 classic PC titles on Steam, GOG and the EA AppThe massive release features seven fully restored Anniversary Editions for Road Rash and Wing CommanderThe preservation effort utilized a newly discovered vault of physical media to rescue and reedit original master sequencesThe video game industry faces a growing cultural crisis as classic titles increasingly risk being lost to time, trapped behind incompatible modern hardware, deprecating physical media and forgotten storage archives. Stepping up to combat this digital decay, Electronic Arts launched 25 classic PC games on Steam for the first time. The drop, which is also available on GOG and the EA App, serves as a crucial preservation milestone that rescues foundational gaming history from technological obsolescence.The sprawling release was sparked by an internal archaeological find. Jim Vessella, a Senior Producer with the EA Partners team, was part of the group that initiated the dedicated game preservation effort at Electronic Arts. That initiative struck gold when the team discovered a physical media vault containing thousands of Betacam, VHS and D1 tapes alongside other assets. Through a meticulous digitization process, EA recovered master Full-Motion Video (FMV) sequences. Using these master tapes, the team reedited the archival footage to restore more than 1,500 scenes in higher resolution.The crown jewels of this archival drop are seven newly restored Anniversary Editions encompassing the motorcycle racer Road Rash and six Wing Commander titles, all priced at $9.99 USD each. These specialized releases maintain the original look and feel of the games while packing in essential quality-of-life updates to improve overall performance and ensure support for modern systems and controls. The 35th Anniversary Editions bundle Wing Commander and Wing Commander II: Vengeance of the Kilrathi. The 30th Anniversary Editions bring back Road Rash, Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger, Wing Commander IV: The Price of Freedom, Wing Commander Prophecy and Privateer 2: The Darkening. In a nod to the dedicated fanbases that kept these universes alive, the updated Wing Commander titles officially incorporate community-made mods.Beyond the flagship restorations, the remainder of the classic games cost $4.99 USF each. The extensive lineup delivers an 11-game dose of the Ultima franchise, spanning Ultima I through IX, including Ultima VII: The Complete Edition and Ultima VIII: Gold Edition, plus Ultima Underworld I and II. Rounding out the 25-game release are several other legacy heavy-hitters pulled directly from the archives, including Wing Commander: Privateer, Wing Commander: Academy, Wing Commander: Armada, Strike Commander, Theme Hospital, Crusader: No Remorse and Crusader: No Regret.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Health & Pandemic.title: Innovative study tests how people respond to flood warnings under pressure
Health & Pandemic.text: As floods become more frequent, severe and widespread, getting people to respond appropriately to flood warnings is more important than ever. New research from the University of Vermont shows that the way flood hazard information is presented can dramatically affect not only whether people make the right decision, but also how quickly they make it. The findings are published in the journal Crisis and Risk Communication.

Health & Pandemic.title: Autistic children benefited from online literacy instruction during COVID pandemic
Health & Pandemic.text: Despite many obstacles presented by students being at home during COVID-19 lockdowns and restrictions, autistic children involved in a feasibility study still showed significant progress through online instruction. Flinders University's Professor Joanne Arciuli, who led the study, says that developing useful tools for this area of literacy teaching plugs a gap in autistic care.

Longevity & Anti-Aging.title: Arguing for a Better Assessment of Lactoferrin as a Geroprotective Supplement
Longevity & Anti-Aging.text: A great many proteins and other molecules might be capable of mild geroprotective effects, slightly slowing aging, or slightly improving late life health. As a general rule, proposed mechanisms for potentially geroprotective effects found in the literature are usually correct. The open question is always the size of the effect produced by those mechanisms in humans. Firm data is usually lacking, and the only practical way to determine outcomes is to run expensive, lengthy clinical studies. Those expensive, lengthy studies are not usually put together for low-cost interventions, and thus the state of uncertainty continues, fueling a supplement industry and anti-aging medical community that runs on marketing rather than facts. Obesity is now known to promote an accelerated age-related accumulation of senescent cells in many tissues. It is not surprising to find cellular senescence in liver cells as an important mechanism in the progression of MASLD to more severe and ultimately fatal liver conditions. Longevity & Anti-Aging.title: Inhibiting the H3K9me3 Epigenetic Modification Reduces Pathology in Mouse Models of Alzheimer's Disease
Longevity & Anti-Aging.text: Nuclear DNA structure determines which genes are transcribed into RNA. The molecules making up the machineries of transcription move around the nucleus to interact with every sequence of DNA they can reach. Regions of DNA that are spooled onto histone molecules and compacted are hidden, and those genes are thus silenced and not expressed. Regions of DNA that are unspooled are accessible to transcription machinery, and those genes are actively expressed. Nuclear DNA structure changes constantly, controlled by the addition and removal of decorating molecules at specific locations on DNA and histones. This is known as epigenetic regulation, a highly complex layer of interaction between cell state and pattern of gene expression. Epigenetic control of DNA structure changes with age.
